Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry o f Earth Sciences, Technical Publication No. 21, pp 155-159
XXIII Indian Antarctic Expedition Hydrographic  
Survey—India Bay
Prashant K. Srivastava & Siva R.K. Kopalli
National Hydrographic Office, Dehradun
INTRODUCTION
The Hydrographic Survey of India Bay, Antarctica HI/NHO/01/2003- 
04 was undertaken during the X X IIIIA  expedition from 05 Dec 03 to 30 
Mar 04. A total of 310 nautical miles of sounding was carried out by the 
expedition team. Apart from the bathymetric survey, current, salinity and 
sound velocity observations were also carried out during the expedition at 
various places. CTD probe was employed for data collection for the first 
time during the survey. The 150 NM ice shelf around the India Bay was 
delineated using System GPS 200 on K inem atic in the Fly mode. 
Meteorological observations were also carried out during the survey.
GEODETIC CONTROL
Horizontal control for the entire survey was established in WGS 84 
Datum and plotted on Mercator Projection with scale true at 66° S. GPS 
coordinates as directly obtained from the ship fitted GPS “Trimble Navtrac 
XL” were used for sounding. No control was established for this purpose. 
However, the output of the ship fitted GPS set was compared with the 
Leica GPS 200 available with the survey team and positions were found to 
be acceptable. The following existing station was recovered and used for 
extension of Geodetic Control. The coordinates of the station in WGS 84 
Datum are as follows:

BATHYMETRY
The bathymetric survey was undertaken using the ship fitted echo 
sounder. Two Russian made echo sounders were available onboard. Model 
M4 designed for measuring depths up to 35 m and model NEL M3B for 
measuring depths up to 500 m. These instruments are analogue in nature 
and have no digital output to log the data in an Automated Survey System. 
In view of this, the data recorded was manually extracted from the analogue 
echo trace using manually graduated scale and corrected for draft and 
calibration. The sound velocity was fixed at 1500 m/s on the echo sounder 
and used for depth data collection. As all the soundings were more than 
200mtrs, they were then corrected for index error of the echo sounder, 
ships draught and sound velocity using the Nautical Publication 139 echo 
sounder correction tables for Antarctic region. The sounding lines were run 
at approximately 1  cm apart on scale the scale of survey (1 :  200,000), 
perpendicular to the depth contours. A cross line was also run in the area. A 
total of 310 Nautical miles of sounding was completed in areas designated 
as A, B and C on chart INT 9051.
COASTAL TOPOGRAPHY AND TOPOGRAPHICAL FEATURES
Delineation of the complete ice shelf was carried out on 15 Mar 04. 
The ice shelf was surveyed using the integral helicopter at an average speed 
of 80 knots and height o f200 feet was maintained during the operation. The 
data was logged on Leica GPS 200 in Kinematic on the Fly mode. The GPS 
data of the IGS Station, DAVIS (Australia) was used as reference for 
processing the logged data. This station was used for baseline measurements 
to the ice shelf. The entire GPS data was processed in baseline mode using 
SKI version 2.3. The graphical representation of the complete ice shelf 
from 11° E to 14° E was plotted on a scale of 1:50 000 (enclosed figure) for 
studying the changes in the ice shelf. The coast or the ice shelf is totally 
barren and desolate. The ice cliff forms the seaward edge of the ice shelf. 
In most locations it is about 10-15 metres above waterline. Extreme caution 
needs to be exercised while moving on the shelf by foot or motorized vehicle. 
These cliffs are extremely dynamic features and are prone to breaking off 
and separating. Although they paint distinctively on radar, they become 
visually distinct only on melting of the fast ice in the summer. There is no 
plantation or vegetation even during the summer. The only feature that at 
times is visual during the summer months are some crevasses. There are 
no conspicuous objects along the coast falling within the survey area. 
However, there are numerous containers lying at the Indian and Russian
